source.title: Conditioning of Random Feature Matrices: Double Descent and Generalization Error

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent in random-feature regression by varying feature count and measuring empirical test risk, rather than testing the claim in deep networks.
record.gate_note: Figure 2.1 reports empirical risk curves for feature-count sweeps; the text states that the curves show double descent and peak at N/m = 1. Other cited results are not this study's results. No epoch or sample-size sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps random-feature count at fixed m=100 and reports empirical test risk peaking at N/m=1 and falling again in the overparameterized regime (Fig. 2.1). It also proves risk bounds on both sides of the threshold. This bears on V4 (double descent beyond deep networks) and, via the zero-noise vs 10% SNR comparison, on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove that the random-feature matrix is well-conditioned when N/m scales like log(m) or 1/log(N), and ill-conditioned at N=m. They argue that risk double descent in random-feature regression is a consequence of condition-number double descent. Risk bounds decrease without regularization, and small risk needs N/m only logarithmically, not algebraically, far from the threshold. Empirically, the risk peaks at N/m=1 and its global minimum is overparameterized.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a shallow random-feature regression model with a fixed randomized feature layer and varies feature count; it is not a test on deep networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports the risk pattern for Fourier features with and without additive noise, and for ReLU features; the ReLU experiment's noise condition is not stated.

fits_no_version.finding: The condition number of the random-feature matrix shows double descent; it is provably ill-conditioned at N=m and well-conditioned when N/m is logarithmically far from 1. Its peak coincides with the empirical risk peak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak in random-feature regression is caused by ill-conditioning of the feature matrix at the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: The empirical risk curves are rescaled, so exact risk values cannot be recovered from the text. Results are averaged over 10 random trials, but uncertainty estimates are not stated. The empirical size sweep uses m = 100 and does not address epochs or sample-size effects.
record.rows_left_out: No additional empirical test-risk results bearing on the tested versions are reported outside Figure 2.1. Condition-number curves are not included as rows because they measure conditioning rather than test risk.

untested.parts: No deep networks; random features with an untrained hidden layer only.
No epoch or training-time sweep; training is a closed-form pseudo-inverse.
m is fixed at 100; no sample-size sweep near the threshold.
Only random-feature regression (Fourier and ReLU features, d=3, linear target); no other model classes.
No test of a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Variance as a mechanism, multiple or triple descent, and the effect of optimally tuned regularization are not tested. The authors leave ridge regression with noise to future work.
Complexity is not recounted with an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Theoretical risk bounds: least-squares risk for m>N (Thm 4.1) and min-norm interpolator risk for m<N (Thm 4.2) are small when N/m is only logarithmically far from 1, without regularization. Together with Thm 3.1(c), this gives a proved double-descent shape. These are theory, not empirical rows.

record.verdict_notes: The study is primarily theoretical; its empirical evidence is a single rescaled figure. It is not among the original sources. The V6 limits_scope label is weak: zero label noise still leaves misspecification error, which V6's 'variance' clause may cover.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test deep networks.
The empirical sweep fixes m at 100; it does not test whether increasing sample size near the threshold raises test error.
Tests random-feature regression, not a broad set of model classes.
Does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Compares zero noise and 10% SNR settings, but does not test variance as a mechanism, multiple or triple descent, or optimally tuned regularization.
Does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters.
